metadata.title: The Entropy of a Binary Hidden Markov Process

extraction_notes.note: Symmetric process P_{+,-}=P_{-,+}=p is both a modelling assumption and the introduction of p; typed definition because p is used throughout.
The Ising (Boltzmann-chain) form of Pr(R,S) is a direct rewriting, cited to Saul-Jordan and MacKay; typed external theorem per the cited-result rule, claim would also fit.
Eq. (33) re-expresses Z(R) in p, epsilon; it is really Q(R) (it already contains the normalisation A), so it is a claim about a re-used symbol rather than a new definition.

Section 3 has no proof environment: the derivation from 'A few technical points' to the colon before (28) is the proof; (28)-(30) form the claimed result. The derivation omits the actual summations ('straightforward, albeit tedious'), hence semi_formal.
The coefficients H^(3)..H^(11) are only in unnumbered $$ displays in the Appendix; emitted as one conjectural claim spanning the Appendix list.
Motivational introduction (communication, compression, error correction), the Omega_S paragraph, captions of the four figures, and the radius-of-convergence motivation sentence have no nodes.

metadata.extraction_comment: Results here are derivations and symbolic/numerical computations rather than theorem-proof; only orders 0-2 are derived, orders 3-11 rest on the settling conjecture (CnjP1).

nodes.name: Number of received signals Omega_R
nodes.statement: For both problem areas it is of central importance to estimate $\Omega_R$, the number of (expected) received signals.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

nodes.name: Omega_R ~ 2^{NH} (typical set size)
nodes.statement: In general, $\Omega_R$ is given, for large $N$, by $2^{NH}$, where $H=H(p,\epsilon)$ is the {\it entropy} of the process.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.statement_short: For long messages the number of received signals is about $2^{NH}$, $H$ the entropy (asymptotic equipartition).

nodes.name: Channel capacity of a Markov source over a noisy channel
nodes.statement: The calculation of channel capacity for a Markovian source transmitted over a noisy channel is still an open question.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

nodes.name: Not the quenched random-field entropy (replica n=1)
nodes.statement: Note that the object we are calculating is {\it not} the entropy of an Ising chain in a quenched random field, as shown in eq. (\ref{H_N_def}) and in the discussion following it. In technical terms, here we set the replica index to $n=1$ after the calculation, whereas to obtain the (quenched average) properties of an Ising chain one works in the $n \rightarrow 0$ limit.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.statement_short: The computed quantity is the replica derivative at $n=1$, not the quenched ($n\to0$) random-field Ising entropy.

nodes.name: Binary transmitted symbols s_i
nodes.statement: Binary valued symbols, $s_i=\pm 1$ are generated and transmitted at fixed times $i \Delta t $.
nodes.section: 2.1 Defining the process and its entropy

nodes.name: Transmitted sequence S
nodes.statement: Denote a sequence of $N$ transmitted symbols by \begin{equation} S = (s_1,s_2,....s_N) \end{equation}

nodes.name: Transmitted sequence S
nodes.section: 2.1 Defining the process and its entropy

nodes.name: Markov source
nodes.statement: The sequence is generated by a Markov process; here we assume that the value of $s_{i+1}$ depends only on $s_i$ (and not on the symbols generated at previous times).
nodes.section: 2.1 Defining the process and its entropy

nodes.name: Transition matrix P
nodes.statement: The process is parametrized by a transition matrix $P$, whose elements are the transition probabilities \begin{equation} P_{+,-}= Pr(s_{i+1}=+1|s_i=-1) \qquad \qquad P_{-,+}= Pr(s_{i+1}=-1|s_i=+1) \end{equation}
nodes.section: 2.1 Defining the process and its entropy

nodes.name: Transition probabilities
nodes.section: 2.1 Defining the process and its entropy

nodes.name: Binary symmetric Markov process (flipping rate p)
nodes.statement: Here we treat the case of a {\it symmetric} process, i.e. $P_{+,-} = P_{-,+}=p,~~$ so that we have \begin{equation} s_{i+1} = \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} ~~ s_i \qquad \qquad & {\rm prob.}= 1-p \\ -s_i \qquad \qquad & {\rm prob.}= p \end{array} \right. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 2.1 Defining the process and its entropy
nodes.statement_short: Symmetric Markov chain: each symbol is flipped relative to the previous one with probability $p$.

nodes.name: Symmetric Markov transition rule
nodes.statement: s_{i+1} = \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} ~~ s_i \qquad \qquad & {\rm prob.}= 1-p \\ -s_i \qquad \qquad & {\rm prob.}= p \end{array} \right.
nodes.section: 2.1 Defining the process and its entropy
nodes.label: eq:Markov

nodes.name: Uniform first symbol
nodes.statement: The first symbol $s_1$ takes the values $\pm 1$ with equal probabilities, $Pr(s_1=+1)=Pr(s_1=-1)=1/2$.
nodes.section: 2.1 Defining the process and its entropy

nodes.name: Probability of a Markov sequence Pr(S)
nodes.statement: Pr(S) = \frac{1}{2}\prod_{i=2}^N Pr(s_i|s_{i-1})
nodes.section: 2.1 Defining the process and its entropy
nodes.label: eq:P(S)

nodes.name: Received sequence R
nodes.statement: The generated sequence $S$ is "{\it sent}" and passes through a noisy channel; hence the {\it received} sequence, \begin{equation} {\it R } = (r_1,r_2,...r_N) \end{equation} is not identical to the transmitted one.

nodes.name: Received sequence R

nodes.name: Binary Symmetric Channel (noise level epsilon)
nodes.statement: The noise can flip a transmitted symbol with probability $\epsilon$: \begin{equation} Pr(r_i=-s_i|s_i)=\epsilon \end{equation}
nodes.section: 2.1 Defining the process and its entropy
also_stated_at: The simplest way to model the noise is known as the {\it Binary Symmetric Channel}, where each bit of the original message is flipped with probability $\epsilon$.

nodes.name: Noise flip probability
nodes.statement: Pr(r_i=-s_i|s_i)=\epsilon
nodes.section: 2.1 Defining the process and its entropy
nodes.label: eq:f

nodes.name: i.i.d. noise
nodes.statement: Here we assumed that the noise is generated by an independent identically distributed (iid) process; the probability of a flip at time $i$ is independent of what happened at other times $j<i$ and of the value of $i$.
nodes.section: 2.1 Defining the process and its entropy

nodes.name: Symmetric noise
nodes.statement: We also assume that the noise is symmetric, i.e. the flip probability does not depend on $s_i$.
nodes.section: 2.1 Defining the process and its entropy

nodes.name: Channel likelihood Pr(R|S)
nodes.statement: Pr({\it R }|S) = \prod_{i=1}^N Pr(r_i|s_i)
nodes.section: 2.1 Defining the process and its entropy
nodes.label: eq:PSig

nodes.name: Joint probability Pr(R,S)
nodes.statement: Pr({\it R }, S) = Pr({\it R }|S)Pr(S)
nodes.section: 2.1 Defining the process and its entropy
nodes.label: eq:joint

nodes.name: Probability of a received signal Q(R)
nodes.statement: Hence it is meaningful to ask - what is the probability to observe any particular received signal ${\it R }$? The answer is \begin{equation} Q({\it R } ) = \sum_S Pr({\it R } , S) \end{equation}
nodes.section: 2.1 Defining the process and its entropy

nodes.name: Output distribution Q(R)
nodes.statement: Q({\it R } ) = \sum_S Pr({\it R } , S)
nodes.section: 2.1 Defining the process and its entropy
nodes.label: eq:QSig

nodes.name: Shannon entropy H_N and entropy rate H
nodes.statement: Furthermore, one is interested in the\footnote{The Shannon entropy is defined using log$_2$; we use natural log for simplicity} {\it Shannon entropy H} of the observed process, \begin{equation} H_N = -\sum_{\it R } Q({\it R }) \log Q({\it R }) \end{equation} and in particular, in the {\it entropy rate}, defined as \begin{equation} H = \lim_{N \rightarrow \infty} \frac{H_N}{N}\end{equation}
nodes.section: 2.1 Defining the process and its entropy

nodes.name: Block entropy H_N
nodes.statement: H_N = -\sum_{\it R } Q({\it R }) \log Q({\it R })
nodes.section: 2.1 Defining the process and its entropy
nodes.label: eq:HN

nodes.name: Entropy rate H
nodes.statement: H = \lim_{N \rightarrow \infty} \frac{H_N}{N}
nodes.section: 2.1 Defining the process and its entropy

nodes.name: Ising couplings J and K
nodes.statement: The conditional Markov probabilities (\ref{eq:Markov}), that connect the symbols from one site to the next, can be rewritten as \begin{equation} Pr(s_{i+1}|s_i) = e^{J s_{i+1}s_i}/(e^J + e^{-J}) \qquad {\rm with} \qquad e^{2J} = (1-p)/p \end{equation} and similarly, the flip probability generated by the noise, (\ref{eq:f}), is also recapitulated by the Ising form \begin{equation} Pr(r_i|s_i)= e^{K r_i s_i}/(e^K+e^{-K}) \qquad {\rm with} \qquad e^{2K}=(1-\epsilon)/\epsilon \end{equation}
nodes.section: 2.2 Casting the problem in Ising form
nodes.statement_short: Write the Markov transition and the noise flip as Ising Boltzmann factors with couplings $e^{2J}=(1-p)/p$, $e^{2K}=(1-\epsilon)/\epsilon$.

nodes.name: Markov coupling J
nodes.statement: Pr(s_{i+1}|s_i) = e^{J s_{i+1}s_i}/(e^J + e^{-J}) \qquad {\rm with} \qquad e^{2J} = (1-p)/p
nodes.section: 2.2 Casting the problem in Ising form
nodes.label: eq:pJ

nodes.name: Noise coupling K
nodes.statement: Pr(r_i|s_i)= e^{K r_i s_i}/(e^K+e^{-K}) \qquad {\rm with} \qquad e^{2K}=(1-\epsilon)/\epsilon
nodes.section: 2.2 Casting the problem in Ising form

nodes.name: Boltzmann-chain form of the HMP joint probability
nodes.statement: The joint probability of realizing a pair of transmitted and observed sequences ($S, {\it R }$) takes the form (\cite{Saul},\cite{MacKay}) \begin{equation} Pr({\it R },S)= A \exp \left( J \sum_{i=1}^{N-1} s_{i+1} s_i + K \sum_{i=1}^N r_i s_i \right) \end{equation} where the constant $A$ is the product of two factors, $A=A_0 A_1$, given by \begin{equation} A_0 = \frac{1}{2} \left( e^J + e^{-J} \right)^{-(N-1)} \qquad \qquad A_1 = \left( e^K + e^{-K} \right)^{-N} \end{equation}
nodes.section: 2.2 Casting the problem in Ising form
nodes.statement_short: The HMP joint law is an Ising chain with couplings $J$ and local fields $K r_i$, normalized by $A=A_0A_1$.
conclusions: Pr({\it R },S)= A \exp \left( J \sum_{i=1}^{N-1} s_{i+1} s_i + K \sum_{i=1}^N r_i s_i \right) \label{eq:prIsing} \end{equation} where the constant $A$ is the product of two factors, $A=A_0 A_1$, given by \begin{equation} A_0 = \frac{1}{2} \left( e^J + e^{-J} \right)^{-(N-1)} \qquad \qquad A_1 = \left( e^K + e^{-K} \right)^{-N}

nodes.name: Ising form of Pr(R,S)
nodes.statement: Pr({\it R },S)= A \exp \left( J \sum_{i=1}^{N-1} s_{i+1} s_i + K \sum_{i=1}^N r_i s_i \right)
nodes.section: 2.2 Casting the problem in Ising form
nodes.label: eq:prIsing

nodes.name: Normalization constants A_0, A_1
nodes.statement: A_0 = \frac{1}{2} \left( e^J + e^{-J} \right)^{-(N-1)} \qquad \qquad A_1 = \left( e^K + e^{-K} \right)^{-N}
nodes.section: 2.2 Casting the problem in Ising form

nodes.name: Ising chain with dangling bonds
nodes.statement: The first sum in (\ref{eq:prIsing}) is the Hamiltonian of a chain of Ising spins with open boundary conditions and nearest neighbor interactions $J$; the interactions are ferromagnetic ($J>0$) for $p < 1/2$. The second term corresponds, for small noise $\epsilon <1/2$, to a strong ferromagnetic interaction $K$ between each spin $s_i$ and another spin, $r_i$, connected to $s_i$ by a "dangling bond" (see Fig 2).
nodes.section: 2.2 Casting the problem in Ising form

nodes.name: Partition sum Z(R) over hidden variables
nodes.statement: Denote the summation over the hidden variables by $Z({\it R })$: \begin{equation} Z({\it R }) = \sum_S \exp \left( J \sum_{i=1}^{N-1} s_{i+1} s_i + K \sum_{i=1}^N r_i s_i \right) \end{equation} so that the probability $Q({\it R })$ becomes (see eq. (\ref{eq:QSig})) $Q({\it R } ) = A~Z({\it R })$.
nodes.section: 2.2 Casting the problem in Ising form

nodes.name: Partition sum Z(R)
nodes.statement: Z({\it R }) = \sum_S \exp \left( J \sum_{i=1}^{N-1} s_{i+1} s_i + K \sum_{i=1}^N r_i s_i \right)
nodes.section: 2.2 Casting the problem in Ising form
nodes.label: eq:ZR

nodes.name: Replica-derivative formula for H_N
nodes.statement: Substituting in (\ref{eq:HN}), the entropy of the process can be written as \begin{equation} H_N = - \sum_{\it R } A~Z({\it R }) \log[A Z({\it R })] = - \left[ \frac{d }{dn} \sum_{\it R } [A~Z({\it R })]^n \right]_{n=1} \end{equation}
nodes.section: 2.2 Casting the problem in Ising form
nodes.statement_short: $H_N$ is minus the $n$-derivative at $n=1$ of $\sum_R [A Z(R)]^n$.
conclusions: H_N = - \sum_{\it R } A~Z({\it R }) \log[A Z({\it R })] = - \left[ \frac{d }{dn} \sum_{\it R } [A~Z({\it R })]^n \right]_{n=1}

nodes.name: H_N as replica derivative
nodes.statement: H_N = - \sum_{\it R } A~Z({\it R }) \log[A Z({\it R })] = - \left[ \frac{d }{dn} \sum_{\it R } [A~Z({\it R })]^n \right]_{n=1}
nodes.section: 2.2 Casting the problem in Ising form
nodes.label: H_N_def

nodes.name: Random-field Ising interpretation
nodes.statement: The interpretation of this expression is obvious: an Ising chain is submitted to local fields $h_i=Kr_i$, with the sign of the field at each site being $\pm$ with equal probabilities, and we have to average $Z(h_1,...h_N)^n$ over the field configurations. This is precisely the problem one faces in order to calculate properties of a well-studied model, of a nearest neighbor Ising chain in a quenched random field of uniform strength and random signs at the different sites (there one is interested, however, in the limit $n \rightarrow 0$).
nodes.section: 2.2 Casting the problem in Ising form
nodes.statement_short: $H_N$ averages $Z^n$ of an Ising chain over random-sign local fields $Kr_i$, as in the quenched RFIM but at $n=1$.

nodes.name: Exact solution of the 1D random-field Ising chain
nodes.statement: This problem has not been solved analytically, albeit a few exactly solvable simplified versions of the model do exist (\cite{Derrida}, \cite{Fisher}, \cite{Grinstein}, \cite{Nieuwenhuizen}), as well as expansions (albeit in the weak field limit \cite{DerHil}).
nodes.section: 2.2 Casting the problem in Ising form
nodes.origin_citation: Derrida et al.; Fisher et al.; Grinstein & Mukamel; Nieuwenhuizen & Luck

nodes.name: Entropy of the field signs, not of the spins
nodes.statement: One should note that here we calculate the entropy associated with the observed variables {\it R }. In the Ising language this corresponds to an entropy associated with the randomly assigned signs of the local fields, and {\it not} to the entropy of the spins $S$. Because of this distinction the entropy $H_N$ has no obvious physical interpretation or relevance, which explains why the problem has not been addressed yet by the physics community.
nodes.section: 2.2 Casting the problem in Ising form

nodes.name: Small noise = infinite field limit
nodes.statement: We are interested in calculating the entropy rate {\it in the limit of small noise}, i.e. $\epsilon \ll 1$. In the Ising representation this limit corresponds to $K \gg 1$ and hence an expansion in $\epsilon$ corresponds to expanding near the infinite field limit of the Ising chain.
nodes.section: 2.2 Casting the problem in Ising form

nodes.name: Entropy rate in Ising form
nodes.statement: H = - \lim_{N \rightarrow \infty}\left[ \frac{1}{N}\sum_{\it R } A~Z({\it R }) \log A~Z({\it R })\right]
nodes.section: 3 Expansion to order $\epsilon^2$: exact results
nodes.label: eq:HI

nodes.name: Low-noise expansion of Z(R) to second order
nodes.statement: A few technical points are in order. First, we will actually use \begin{equation} e^{-2K}=\epsilon/(1-\epsilon) \end{equation} as our small parameter and expand to order $\epsilon^2$ afterwards. Second, we will calculate $H_N$ and take the large $N$ limit. Therefore we can replace the open boundary conditions with periodic ones (setting $s_{N+1}=s_1$) - the difference is a surface effect of order $1/N$. The constant $A_0$ becomes \begin{equation} A_0 =\left( e^J + e^{-J} \right)^{-N} \end{equation} and the interaction term $J s_1s_N$ is added to the first sum in eq. (\ref{eq:prIsing}), which contains now $N$ pairs of neighbors. {\bf Expanding $Z({\it R })$:} Consider $Z({\it R } )$ from (\ref{eq:ZR}). For any fixed {\it R }$=(r_1,r_2,...r_N)$ the leading order is obtained by the $S$ configuration with $s_i=r_i$ for all $i$. For this configuration each site contributes $K$ to the "field term" in (\ref{eq:ZR}). The contribution of this configuration to the summation over $S$ in (\ref{eq:ZR}) is \begin{equation} Z({\it R })^{(0)} = e^{NK} \exp \left( J \sum_{i=1}^N r_{i+1} r_i \right) \end{equation} The next term we add consists of the contributions of those $S$ configurations which have $s_i=r_i$ at {\it all but one position}. The field term of such a configuration is $K$ from $N-1$ sites and $-K$ from the single site with $s_j=-r_j$. There are $N$ such configurations, and the total contribution of these terms to the sum (\ref{eq:ZR}) is \begin{equation} Z({\it R })^{(1)} = e^{NK}e^{-2K} \exp \left( J \sum_{i=1}^N r_{i+1} r_i \right) \sum_{j=1}^N \exp [-2J r_j(r_{j-1}+r_{j+1})] \end{equation} The next term is of the highest order studied in this paper; it involves configurations $S$ with all but two spins in the state $s_i=r_i$; the other two take the values $s_j=-r_j,~~ s_k=-r_k$, i.e. are flipped with respect to the corresponding local fields. These $S$ configurations belong to one of two classes. In class $a$ the two flipped spins are located on nearest neighbor sites, e.g. $k=j+1$; there are $N$ such configurations. To the second class, $b$, belong those configurations in which the two flipped spins are {\it not} neighbors - there are $N(N-3)/2$ such terms in the sum (\ref{eq:ZR}), and the respective contributions are\footnote{ We use the obvious identifications imposed by periodic boundary conditions, e.g. $r_{N+1}=r_1,~~r_{N+2}=r_2$} \begin{equation} Z({\it R })^{(2a)} = e^{NK}e^{-4K} \exp \left( J \sum_{i=1}^N r_{i+1} r_i \right) \sum_{j=1}^N \exp [-2J (r_jr_{j-1}+r_{j+1}r_{j+2})] \end{equation} \begin{equation} Z({\it R })^{(2b)} = e^{NK}e^{-4K} \exp \left( J \sum_{i=1}^N r_{i+1} r_i \right) \frac{1}{2}\sum_{j=1}^N \sum_{k \neq j,j\pm1} \exp [-2J r_j(r_{j-1}+r_{j+1}) - 2J r_k(r_{k-1}+r_{k+1})] \end{equation} Calculation of $H$ is now straightforward, albeit tedious: substitute $AZ$ into eq. (\ref{eq:HI}), expand everything in powers of $\epsilon$, to second order, and for each term perform the summation over all the $r_i$ variables. These summations involve two kinds of terms. The first is of the "partition-sum-like" form \begin{equation} \sum_R e^{{\cal H}(R)} \qquad {\rm where} \qquad {\cal H}(R)=\sum_j \Delta_j J r_j r_{j+1} \qquad {\rm with} \qquad \Delta_j=\pm 1 \end{equation} For the case studied here we encounter either all bonds $\Delta_j J>0$, or two have a flipped sign (corresponding to eq. (\ref{eq:Z1}, \ref{eq:Z2a})), or four have flipped signs (corresponding to (\ref{eq:Z2b})). These "partition-sum-like" terms are independent of the signs of the $\Delta_j$; in fact we have for all of them \begin{equation} A_0 \sum_R e^{{\cal H}(R)} =1 \end{equation} The second type of term that contributes to $H$ is of the "energy-like" form: \begin{equation} \sum_R e^{{\cal H}(R)} r_k r_{k+1} \end{equation} The absolute value of these terms is again independent of the $\Delta_j$, but one has to keep track of their signs. Finally, one has to remember that the constant $A_1$ also has to be expanded in $\epsilon$. The calculation finally yields the following result (here we switch from $J$ to the "natural" variable $p$ using eq. (\ref{eq:pJ})):
nodes.section: 3 Expansion to order $\epsilon^2$: exact results
nodes.statement_short: High-field expansion: expand $Z(R)$ by the number of spins flipped against their fields (0, 1, 2 adjacent or not), then sum over $R$ using partition-sum-like and energy-like identities. The key step is that every partition-sum-like term normalizes to $A_0\sum_R e^{\cal H}=1$.

nodes.name: Zeroth-order term Z^(0)
nodes.statement: Consider $Z({\it R } )$ from (\ref{eq:ZR}). For any fixed {\it R }$=(r_1,r_2,...r_N)$ the leading order is obtained by the $S$ configuration with $s_i=r_i$ for all $i$. For this configuration each site contributes $K$ to the "field term" in (\ref{eq:ZR}). The contribution of this configuration to the summation over $S$ in (\ref{eq:ZR}) is \begin{equation} Z({\it R })^{(0)} = e^{NK} \exp \left( J \sum_{i=1}^N r_{i+1} r_i \right) \end{equation}
nodes.section: 3 Expansion to order $\epsilon^2$: exact results
nodes.statement_short: Leading term: all spins aligned with their fields

nodes.name: First-order term Z^(1)
nodes.statement: The next term we add consists of the contributions of those $S$ configurations which have $s_i=r_i$ at {\it all but one position}. The field term of such a configuration is $K$ from $N-1$ sites and $-K$ from the single site with $s_j=-r_j$. There are $N$ such configurations, and the total contribution of these terms to the sum (\ref{eq:ZR}) is \begin{equation} Z({\it R })^{(1)} = e^{NK}e^{-2K} \exp \left( J \sum_{i=1}^N r_{i+1} r_i \right) \sum_{j=1}^N \exp [-2J r_j(r_{j-1}+r_{j+1})] \end{equation}
nodes.section: 3 Expansion to order $\epsilon^2$: exact results
nodes.statement_short: One spin flipped: $N$ configurations with weight $e^{-2K}$

nodes.name: Second-order terms Z^(2a), Z^(2b)
nodes.statement: The next term is of the highest order studied in this paper; it involves configurations $S$ with all but two spins in the state $s_i=r_i$; the other two take the values $s_j=-r_j,~~ s_k=-r_k$, i.e. are flipped with respect to the corresponding local fields. These $S$ configurations belong to one of two classes. In class $a$ the two flipped spins are located on nearest neighbor sites, e.g. $k=j+1$; there are $N$ such configurations. To the second class, $b$, belong those configurations in which the two flipped spins are {\it not} neighbors - there are $N(N-3)/2$ such terms in the sum (\ref{eq:ZR}), and the respective contributions are\footnote{ We use the obvious identifications imposed by periodic boundary conditions, e.g. $r_{N+1}=r_1,~~r_{N+2}=r_2$} \begin{equation} Z({\it R })^{(2a)} = e^{NK}e^{-4K} \exp \left( J \sum_{i=1}^N r_{i+1} r_i \right) \sum_{j=1}^N \exp [-2J (r_jr_{j-1}+r_{j+1}r_{j+2})] \end{equation} \begin{equation} Z({\it R })^{(2b)} = e^{NK}e^{-4K} \exp \left( J \sum_{i=1}^N r_{i+1} r_i \right) \frac{1}{2}\sum_{j=1}^N \sum_{k \neq j,j\pm1} \exp [-2J r_j(r_{j-1}+r_{j+1}) - 2J r_k(r_{k-1}+r_{k+1})] \end{equation}
nodes.section: 3 Expansion to order $\epsilon^2$: exact results
nodes.statement_short: Two flipped spins: adjacent (class a) or not (class b)

nodes.name: Substitute and expand
nodes.statement: Calculation of $H$ is now straightforward, albeit tedious: substitute $AZ$ into eq. (\ref{eq:HI}), expand everything in powers of $\epsilon$, to second order, and for each term perform the summation over all the $r_i$ variables.
nodes.section: 3 Expansion to order $\epsilon^2$: exact results
nodes.statement_short: Substitute $AZ$ into the entropy, expand to second order and sum over $r_i$

nodes.name: Partition-sum-like terms
nodes.statement: These summations involve two kinds of terms. The first is of the "partition-sum-like" form \begin{equation} \sum_R e^{{\cal H}(R)} \qquad {\rm where} \qquad {\cal H}(R)=\sum_j \Delta_j J r_j r_{j+1} \qquad {\rm with} \qquad \Delta_j=\pm 1 \end{equation} For the case studied here we encounter either all bonds $\Delta_j J>0$, or two have a flipped sign (corresponding to eq. (\ref{eq:Z1}, \ref{eq:Z2a})), or four have flipped signs (corresponding to (\ref{eq:Z2b})). These "partition-sum-like" terms are independent of the signs of the $\Delta_j$; in fact we have for all of them \begin{equation} A_0 \sum_R e^{{\cal H}(R)} =1 \end{equation}
nodes.section: 3 Expansion to order $\epsilon^2$: exact results
nodes.statement_short: Partition-sum-like terms all normalize: $A_0\sum_R e^{{\cal H}(R)}=1$

nodes.name: Energy-like terms
nodes.statement: The second type of term that contributes to $H$ is of the "energy-like" form: \begin{equation} \sum_R e^{{\cal H}(R)} r_k r_{k+1} \end{equation} The absolute value of these terms is again independent of the $\Delta_j$, but one has to keep track of their signs.
nodes.section: 3 Expansion to order $\epsilon^2$: exact results
nodes.statement_short: Energy-like terms have $\Delta$-independent magnitude; track their signs

nodes.name: Expand A_1 and collect
nodes.statement: Finally, one has to remember that the constant $A_1$ also has to be expanded in $\epsilon$. The calculation finally yields the following result (here we switch from $J$ to the "natural" variable $p$ using eq. (\ref{eq:pJ})):
nodes.section: 3 Expansion to order $\epsilon^2$: exact results
nodes.statement_short: Expand $A_1$ in $\epsilon$ and collect terms, switching from $J$ to $p$

nodes.name: Zeroth-order term Z^(0)
nodes.statement: Z({\it R })^{(0)} = e^{NK} \exp \left( J \sum_{i=1}^N r_{i+1} r_i \right)
nodes.section: 3 Expansion to order $\epsilon^2$: exact results
nodes.label: eq:Z0

nodes.name: First-order term Z^(1)
nodes.statement: Z({\it R })^{(1)} = e^{NK}e^{-2K} \exp \left( J \sum_{i=1}^N r_{i+1} r_i \right) \sum_{j=1}^N \exp [-2J r_j(r_{j-1}+r_{j+1})]
nodes.section: 3 Expansion to order $\epsilon^2$: exact results
nodes.label: eq:Z1

nodes.name: Second-order term Z^(2a)
nodes.statement: Z({\it R })^{(2a)} = e^{NK}e^{-4K} \exp \left( J \sum_{i=1}^N r_{i+1} r_i \right) \sum_{j=1}^N \exp [-2J (r_jr_{j-1}+r_{j+1}r_{j+2})]
nodes.section: 3 Expansion to order $\epsilon^2$: exact results
nodes.label: eq:Z2a

nodes.name: Second-order term Z^(2b)
nodes.statement: Z({\it R })^{(2b)} = e^{NK}e^{-4K} \exp \left( J \sum_{i=1}^N r_{i+1} r_i \right) \frac{1}{2}\sum_{j=1}^N \sum_{k \neq j,j\pm1} \exp [-2J r_j(r_{j-1}+r_{j+1}) - 2J r_k(r_{k-1}+r_{k+1})]
nodes.section: 3 Expansion to order $\epsilon^2$: exact results
nodes.label: eq:Z2b

nodes.name: Partition-sum-like terms
nodes.statement: \sum_R e^{{\cal H}(R)} \qquad {\rm where} \qquad {\cal H}(R)=\sum_j \Delta_j J r_j r_{j+1} \qquad {\rm with} \qquad \Delta_j=\pm 1
nodes.section: 3 Expansion to order $\epsilon^2$: exact results

nodes.name: Normalization of partition-sum-like terms
nodes.statement: A_0 \sum_R e^{{\cal H}(R)} =1
nodes.section: 3 Expansion to order $\epsilon^2$: exact results

nodes.name: Energy-like terms
nodes.statement: \sum_R e^{{\cal H}(R)} r_k r_{k+1}
nodes.section: 3 Expansion to order $\epsilon^2$: exact results

nodes.name: Entropy rate of the binary symmetric HMP to second order in epsilon
nodes.statement: \begin{equation} H(p,\epsilon) = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} H^{(k)}(p) \epsilon^k \end{equation} with the coefficients $H_k$ given by : \begin{equation} H^{(0)} = -p \log p - (1-p) \log(1-p) \qquad \qquad H^{(1)} = 2 (1-2p) \log \left[ \frac{1-p}{p} \right] \end{equation} \begin{equation} H^{(2)} = -2(1-2p) \log \left[ \frac{1-p}{p} \right] -\frac{(1-2p)^2}{2p^2(1-p)^2} \end{equation}
nodes.section: 3 Expansion to order $\epsilon^2$: exact results
also_stated_at: We map the problem onto a one-dimensional Ising model in a large field of random signs and calculate the expansion coefficients up to second order in $\epsilon$.
Using a low-temperature/high-random-field expansion we calculated the entropy of the {\it HMP} to second order $k=2$ in the noise parameter $\epsilon$.
nodes.statement_short: Low-noise expansion $H=\sum_k H^{(k)}(p)\epsilon^k$ with explicit $H^{(0)}, H^{(1)}$ and the new second-order coefficient $H^{(2)}$.

nodes.name: Low-noise series for H(p, epsilon)
nodes.statement: H(p,\epsilon) = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} H^{(k)}(p) \epsilon^k
nodes.section: 3 Expansion to order $\epsilon^2$: exact results
nodes.label: eq:exp

nodes.name: Zeroth and first order entropy coefficients
nodes.statement: H^{(0)} = -p \log p - (1-p) \log(1-p) \qquad \qquad H^{(1)} = 2 (1-2p) \log \left[ \frac{1-p}{p} \right]
nodes.section: 3 Expansion to order $\epsilon^2$: exact results
nodes.label: eq:H1H2

nodes.name: Second order entropy coefficient H^(2)
nodes.section: 3 Expansion to order $\epsilon^2$: exact results
nodes.label: 012_stat

nodes.name: Attribution of H^(0), H^(1); H^(2) new
nodes.statement: The zeroth and first order terms (\ref{eq:H1H2}) were known (\cite{Jacquet}, \cite{Weissman:02}), while the second order term is new \cite{ZKD1}.
nodes.section: 3 Expansion to order $\epsilon^2$: exact results
also_stated_at: While the zeroth and first order terms were previously known (\cite{Jacquet}, \cite{Weissman:02}), the second order term was not \cite{ZKD1} .

nodes.name: Conditional entropy C_N
nodes.statement: When investigating the limit $H$, it is useful to study the quantity $C_N = H_N - H_{N-1}$, which is also known as the {\it conditional} entropy.
nodes.section: 4 Upper Bounds derived using a system of finite length

nodes.name: Entropy rate as limit of conditional entropies
nodes.statement: Provided that $H$ exist, it easily follows that \begin{equation} H = \lim_{N \to \infty} C_N \end{equation}
nodes.section: 4 Upper Bounds derived using a system of finite length

nodes.name: H = lim C_N
nodes.statement: H = \lim_{N \to \infty} C_N
nodes.section: 4 Upper Bounds derived using a system of finite length

nodes.name: Conditional entropy upper bound, monotone convergence
nodes.statement: Moreover, according to \cite{Cover}, $C_N \geq H$, and the convergence is monotone : \begin{equation} C_N \searrow H \quad (N \to \infty) \end{equation}
nodes.section: 4 Upper Bounds derived using a system of finite length

nodes.name: C_N decreases to H
nodes.statement: C_N \searrow H \quad (N \to \infty)
nodes.section: 4 Upper Bounds derived using a system of finite length

nodes.name: Z(R) as a polynomial in p and epsilon
nodes.statement: We can express $C_N$ as a function of $p$ and $\epsilon$ by using eq. (\ref{H_N_def}). For this, we represent $Z$ using the original variables $p, {\epsilon }$ (note that from this point of we work with open boundary conditions on the Ising chain of $N$ spins): \begin{equation} Z(R) = \sum_S (1-p)^{\sum_{i=1}^{N-1} 1_{S_i = S_{i+1}}} p^{N-1-\sum_{i=1}^{N-1} 1_{S_i = S_{i+1}}} (1-{\epsilon })^{\sum_{i=1}^N 1_{S_i = R_i}} {\epsilon }^{N-\sum_{i=1}^n 1_{S_i = R_i}} \end{equation} \noindent where we denote $1_{s,s'}=(1+s s')/2$.
nodes.section: 4 Upper Bounds derived using a system of finite length
assumptions: from this point of we work with open boundary conditions on the Ising chain of $N$ spins
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite $Z(R)$ with the original parameters $p,\epsilon$ by counting agreeing neighbours and agreeing symbol pairs.

nodes.name: Z(R) in p, epsilon variables
nodes.section: 4 Upper Bounds derived using a system of finite length
nodes.label: prob_R_cs_style

nodes.name: Coefficients Z_i(R) of the epsilon-polynomial
nodes.statement: Eq. (\ref{prob_R_cs_style}) gives $Z(R)$ explicitly as a polynomial in $p$ and ${\epsilon }$ with maximal degree $N$, and can be represented as : \begin{equation} Z(R) = \sum_{i=0}^N Z_{i} (R) {\epsilon }^i \end{equation} \noindent Here $Z_{i} = Z_{i}(R)$ are functions of $p$ only.
nodes.section: 4 Upper Bounds derived using a system of finite length

nodes.name: Z(R) = sum Z_i epsilon^i
nodes.statement: Z(R) = \sum_{i=0}^N Z_{i} (R) {\epsilon }^i
nodes.section: 4 Upper Bounds derived using a system of finite length
nodes.label: Q_def

nodes.name: Taylor expansion of H_N in epsilon
nodes.statement: Substituting this expansion in eq. (\ref{H_N_def}), and expanding $\log Z(R)$ according to the Taylor series $\log(a+x) = \log(a) - \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{(-x)^n}{n a^n}$, we get \begin{equation} H_N = -\sum_{R} \left[ \sum_{i=0}^N Z_{i} (R) {\epsilon }^i \right] \Biggl[ \log Z_0(R) - \Biggr. \left. \sum_{j=1}^k \frac{ (-\sum_{i=1}^n Z_{i} (R) {\epsilon }^i)^j }{j Z_0 (R)^j} \right] + O({\epsilon }^{k+1}) \end{equation}
nodes.section: 4 Upper Bounds derived using a system of finite length
nodes.statement_short: Taylor-expanding $\log Z(R)$ around $Z_0(R)$ gives $H_N$ to order $\epsilon^k$.
conclusions: H_N = -\sum_{R} \left[ \sum_{i=0}^N Z_{i} (R) {\epsilon }^i \right] \Biggl[ \log Z_0(R) - \Biggr. \left. \sum_{j=1}^k \frac{ (-\sum_{i=1}^n Z_{i} (R) {\epsilon }^i)^j }{j Z_0 (R)^j} \right] + O({\epsilon }^{k+1})

nodes.name: Order-k expansion of H_N
nodes.statement: H_N = -\sum_{R} \left[ \sum_{i=0}^N Z_{i} (R) {\epsilon }^i \right] \Biggl[ \log Z_0(R) - \Biggr. \left. \sum_{j=1}^k \frac{ (-\sum_{i=1}^n Z_{i} (R) {\epsilon }^i)^j }{j Z_0 (R)^j} \right] + O({\epsilon }^{k+1})
nodes.section: 4 Upper Bounds derived using a system of finite length

nodes.name: Expansion coefficients C_N^(i) of the upper bound
nodes.statement: When extended to terms of order $\epsilon^k$, this equation gives us precisely the expansion of the upper-bound $C_N$ up to the {\it k-th} order, \begin{equation} C_N = \sum_{i=0}^{k} C_N^{(i)}{\epsilon }^i + O({\epsilon }^{k+1}) \end{equation}
nodes.section: 4 Upper Bounds derived using a system of finite length

nodes.name: Series for C_N
nodes.statement: C_N = \sum_{i=0}^{k} C_N^{(i)}{\epsilon }^i + O({\epsilon }^{k+1})
nodes.section: 4 Upper Bounds derived using a system of finite length

nodes.name: Second-order expansion of H_N
nodes.statement: For example, stopping at order $L=2$ gives $$ H_N = - \sum_{Y} \biggl\{ Z_0(R) \log Z_0(R) + \biggr. \left[ Z_1(R) (1 + \log Z_0(R)) \right] {\epsilon } + $$ \begin{equation} \left. \left[ \frac{Z_1(R)^2}{2Z_0(R)} + Z_2(R) (1 + \log Z_0(R)) \right] {\epsilon }^2 \right\}+ O({\epsilon }^3) \end{equation}
nodes.section: 4 Upper Bounds derived using a system of finite length

nodes.name: H_N to second order
nodes.statement: \left. \left[ \frac{Z_1(R)^2}{2Z_0(R)} + Z_2(R) (1 + \log Z_0(R)) \right] {\epsilon }^2 \right\}+ O({\epsilon }^3)
nodes.section: 4 Upper Bounds derived using a system of finite length
nodes.label: entropy_expansion

nodes.name: Symbolic computation for N <= 8, k <= 11
nodes.statement: The zeroth and first order terms can be evaluated analytically for any $N$; beyond first order, we can compute the expansion of $H_N$ symbolically \footnote{The computation we have done is exponential in $N$, but the complexity can be improved. } (using Maple \cite{Maple}), for any finite $N$. This was actually done, for $N \leq 8$ and $k \leq 11$.
nodes.section: 4 Upper Bounds derived using a system of finite length
nodes.statement_short: Orders 0 and 1 are analytic for all $N$; higher orders computed symbolically in Maple for $N\le 8$, $k\le 11$.

nodes.name: First-order coefficient C_N^(1) independent of N
nodes.statement: For the first order we have proved (\cite{ZKD1}) that $C_N^{(1)}$ is independent of $N$ (and equals $H^{(1)}$).
nodes.section: 4 Upper Bounds derived using a system of finite length

nodes.name: Observed settling of C_N^(k) at N = ceil((k+3)/2)
nodes.statement: The symbolic computation of higher order terms yielded similar independence of $N$, provided that $N$ is large enough. So, $C_N^{(k)} = C^{(k)}$ for large enough $N$. For example, $C_N^{(2)}$ is independent of $N$ for $3 \leq N \leq 8$ and equals the exact value of $H^{(2)}$ as given by eq. (\ref{012_stat}). Similarly, $C_N^{(4)}$ settles, for $N \geq 4$, at some value denote by $C^{(4)}$, and so on. For the values we have checked, the settling point for $C_N^{(k)}$ turned out to be at $N=\lceil \frac{k+3}{2} \rceil$.
nodes.section: 4 Upper Bounds derived using a system of finite length
assumptions: For the values we have checked
nodes.statement_short: Symbolically, $C_N^{(k)}$ becomes independent of $N$ from $N=\lceil (k+3)/2\rceil$; $C^{(2)}$ equals the exact $H^{(2)}$.
conclusions: the settling point for $C_N^{(k)}$ turned out to be at $N=\lceil \frac{k+3}{2} \rceil$
also_stated_at: We have shown for $k \leq 11$ that when the known upper bound on the entropy rate is expanded in ${\epsilon }$, using finite chains of length $N$, the expansion coefficients settle, for $N_c(k) \leq N \leq 8$, to values that are independent of $N$.

nodes.name: Critical chain length conjecture (settling of C_N^(k))
nodes.statement: For any order $k$, there is a critical chain length $N_c(k)=\lceil \frac{k+3}{2} \rceil$ such that for $N>N_c(k)$ we have $C_N^{(k)} = C^{(k)}$.
nodes.section: 4 Upper Bounds derived using a system of finite length
nodes.statement_short: For each order $k$, the $\epsilon^k$ coefficient of the conditional-entropy bound $C_N$ stops depending on $N$ once $N>\lceil (k+3)/2\rceil$.
conclusions: there is a critical chain length $N_c(k)=\lceil \frac{k+3}{2} \rceil$ such that for $N>N_c(k)$ we have $C_N^{(k)} = C^{(k)}$
also_stated_at: Posing a conjecture, that this continues to hold for any $N$, we identified the expansion coefficients of the entropy up to order 11.

nodes.name: C_N^(k) converges to H^(k)
nodes.statement: It is known that $C_N \to H$, and $C_N$ and $H$ are analytic functions of ${\epsilon }$ at ${\epsilon }=0$ \footnote{See next section on the Radius of Convergence}, so that we can expand both sides around ${\epsilon } = 0$, and conclude that $C_N^{(k)} \to H^{(k)}$ for any $k \geq 1$ when $N \to \infty$.
nodes.section: 4 Upper Bounds derived using a system of finite length
assumptions: $C_N$ and $H$ are analytic functions of ${\epsilon }$ at ${\epsilon }=0$
nodes.statement_short: Since $C_N\to H$ and both are analytic at $\epsilon=0$, the Taylor coefficients converge: $C_N^{(k)}\to H^{(k)}$.

nodes.name: Conjecture implies H^(k) = C^(k)
nodes.statement: Therefore, if our conjecture is true, and $C_N^{(k)}$ indeed settles at some value $C^{(k)}$ independent of $N$ (for $N>N_c(k)$ ), it immediately follows that this value equals $H^{(k)}$.
nodes.section: 4 Upper Bounds derived using a system of finite length
nodes.statement_short: If the settling conjecture holds, the settled coefficient $C^{(k)}$ is the true entropy coefficient $H^{(k)}$.
assumptions: $C_N^{(k)}$ indeed settles at some value $C^{(k)}$ independent of $N$ (for $N>N_c(k)$ )

nodes.name: Evidence for the conjecture at k = 0, 1, 2
nodes.statement: Note that the settling is rigourously supported for $k=0,1$, while for $k=2$ we showed that indeed $C^{(2)}=H^{(2)}$, supporting our conjecture.
nodes.section: 4 Upper Bounds derived using a system of finite length

nodes.name: lambda = 1 - 2p (second eigenvalue of P)
nodes.statement: The first orders up to $H^{(11)}$, obtained by identifying $H^{(k)}$ with $C^{(k)}$, are given in the Appendix, as functions of $\lambda= 1-2p$, for better readability.
nodes.section: 4 Upper Bounds derived using a system of finite length

nodes.name: Agreement with rigorous low-order coefficients
nodes.statement: The values of $H^{(0)},H^{(1)}$ and $H^{(2)}$ coincide with the results that were derived rigorously from the low-temperature/high-field expansion, thus giving us support for postulating the above Conjecture.
nodes.section: 4 Upper Bounds derived using a system of finite length

nodes.name: Observed structure of the coefficients H^(k)
nodes.statement: Interestingly, the nominators have a simpler expression when considered as a functions of $\lambda$, which is the second eigenvalue of the Markov transition matrix $P$. Note that only even powers of $\lambda$ appear. Another interesting observation is that the free element in $[p(1-p)]^{2(k-1)} H^{(k)}$ (when treated as a polynomial in $p$), is $\frac{(-1)^k}{k(k-1)}$, which might suggest some role for the function $\log(1+\frac{{\epsilon }}{[2p(1-p)]^2})$ in the first derivative of $H$.
nodes.section: 4 Upper Bounds derived using a system of finite length
nodes.statement_short: Numerators are simpler in $\lambda$, contain only even powers, and the free term of $[p(1-p)]^{2(k-1)}H^{(k)}$ is claimed to be $(-1)^k/(k(k-1))$.

nodes.name: Rational form of H^(k) in lambda
nodes.statement: All of the above observations led us to conjecture the following form for $H^{(k)}$ (for $k \geq 3$) : \begin{equation} H^{(k)} = \frac{2^{4(k-1)} \sum_{j=0}^{d_k} a_{j,k} \lambda^{2j} }{ k(k-1) (1-\lambda^2)^{2(k-1)}} \end{equation} where $a_{j,k}$ and $d_k$ are integers that can be seen in the Appendix for $H^{(k)}$ up to $k=11$.
nodes.section: 4 Upper Bounds derived using a system of finite length
nodes.statement_short: For $k\ge3$, $H^{(k)}$ is $2^{4(k-1)}$ times an even integer polynomial in $\lambda$ over $k(k-1)(1-\lambda^2)^{2(k-1)}$.

nodes.name: Conjectured form of H^(k)
nodes.section: 4 Upper Bounds derived using a system of finite length

nodes.name: H is not analytic at epsilon = 0 when p = 0
nodes.statement: The fundamental observation made here is that for $p=0$, the function $H({\epsilon })$ is not an analytic function at ${\epsilon } = 0$, since its first derivative diverges.
nodes.section: 5 The Radius of Convergence
conclusions: the function $H({\epsilon })$ is not an analytic function at ${\epsilon } = 0$

nodes.name: Singularity moves to negative epsilon as p grows
nodes.statement: As we increase $p$, the singularity points 'moves' to negative values of ${\epsilon }$, and hence the function is analytic at ${\epsilon } = 0$, but the radius of convergence is determined by the distance of ${\epsilon } = 0$ from this singularity.
nodes.section: 5 The Radius of Convergence

nodes.name: Radius of convergence rho(p)
nodes.statement: Denote by $\rho(p)$ the radius of convergence of $H({\epsilon })$ for a given $p$; we expect that $\rho(p)$ grows when we increase $p$, while for $p \to 0$, $\rho(p) \to 0$.
nodes.section: 5 The Radius of Convergence

nodes.name: Non-interacting i.i.d. model
nodes.statement: It is useful to first look at a simpler model, in which there is no interaction between the spins. Instead, each spin is in an external field which has a uniform constant component $J$, and a site-dependent component of absolute value $K$ and a random sign.
nodes.section: 5 The Radius of Convergence

nodes.name: Entropy rate of the i.i.d. model
nodes.statement: For this simple i.i.d. model the entropy rate takes the form \begin{equation} H = h_b[p(1-{\epsilon })+ {\epsilon }(1-p)] \end{equation} \noindent where $h_b[x] = -[x \log x + (1-x) \log (1-x)]$ is the binary entropy function.
nodes.section: 5 The Radius of Convergence

nodes.name: i.i.d. model entropy rate
nodes.statement: H = h_b[p(1-{\epsilon })+ {\epsilon }(1-p)]
nodes.section: 5 The Radius of Convergence
nodes.label: entropy_iid

nodes.name: Series expansion of the i.i.d. entropy rate
nodes.statement: Expanding eq. (\ref{entropy_iid}) in ${\epsilon }$ (for $p > 0$) gives : $$ H = -(p \log p + (1-p) \log (1-p)) + (1-2p) \log (\frac{1-p}{p}) {\epsilon } + $$ \begin{equation} \sum_{k=2}^{\infty} \frac{1}{k(k-1)} \left[ \frac{(2p-1)^k}{p^k} + \frac{(1-2p)^k}{(1-p)^{k-1}} \right] {\epsilon }^k \end{equation}
nodes.section: 5 The Radius of Convergence
nodes.statement_short: Closed-form Taylor coefficients in $\epsilon$ of $h_b[p+\epsilon(1-2p)]$.

nodes.name: i.i.d. entropy series
nodes.statement: \sum_{k=2}^{\infty} \frac{1}{k(k-1)} \left[ \frac{(2p-1)^k}{p^k} + \frac{(1-2p)^k}{(1-p)^{k-1}} \right] {\epsilon }^k
nodes.section: 5 The Radius of Convergence

nodes.name: Radius of convergence of the i.i.d. model is p/(1-2p)
nodes.statement: The radius of convergence here is easily shown to be $p/(1-2p)$; it goes to 0 for $p \rightarrow 0$ and increases monotonically with $p$.
nodes.section: 5 The Radius of Convergence
conclusions: The radius of convergence here is easily shown to be $p/(1-2p)$

nodes.name: HMP radius expected smaller than i.i.d.
nodes.statement: Returning to the {\it HMP}, the orders $H^{(k)}$ are (in absolute value) usually larger than those of the simpler i.i.d. model, and hence the radius of convergence may be expected to be smaller.
nodes.section: 5 The Radius of Convergence

nodes.name: Ratio-fit extrapolation of the radius of convergence
nodes.statement: Since we could not derive $\rho(p)$ analytically, we estimated it using extrapolation based on the first $11$ orders. We use the fact that $\rho(p) = \lim_{k \to \infty} \frac{H^{(k)}}{H^{(k+1)}}$ (provided the limit exists). The data was fitted to a rational function of the following form (which holds for the i.i.d. model): \begin{equation} \frac{H^{(k)}}{H^{(k+1)}} \sim \frac{a k + b}{k + c}, \end{equation} \noindent For a given fit, the radius of convergence was simply estimated by $a$.

nodes.name: Estimated HMP radius of convergence
nodes.statement: The resulting prediction is given in Fig. \ref{ConvergenceRadius_fig} for both the i.i.d. model (for which it is compared to the known exact $\rho(p)$) and for the {\it HMP}. While quantitatively, the predicted radius of the {\it HMP} is much smaller than this of the i.i.d. model, it has the same qualitative behavior, of starting at zero for $p=0$, and increasing with $p$.

nodes.name: Accuracy of the 11-order series vs. Cover-Thomas bounds
nodes.statement: We compared the analytic expansion to estimates of the entropy rate based on the lower and upper bounds, for two values of ${\epsilon }$ (see Fig. \ref{OrdersApproximationTwoEps_fig}) . First we took ${\epsilon } = 0.01$, which is realistic in typical communication applications. For $p$ less than about 0.1 this value of ${\epsilon }$ exceeds the radius of convergence and the series expansion diverges, whereas for larger $p$ the series converges and gives a very good approximation to $H(p, {\epsilon }=0.01)$. The second value used was ${\epsilon } = 0.2$; here the divergence happens for $p \leq 0.37$, so the expansion yields a good approximation for a much smaller range. We note that, as expected, the approximation is much closer to the upper bound than to the lower bound of \cite{Cover}.
nodes.section: 5 The Radius of Convergence
nodes.statement_short: At $\epsilon=0.01$ the series is accurate for $p\gtrsim0.1$, at $\epsilon=0.2$ only for $p>0.37$; it lies near the upper bound.
